articles.sourceTitle: OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room
articles.title: OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room
articles.text: An OpenAI engineer has been arrested on suspicion of hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters, federal prosecutors said Tuesday.Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday and remains in custody. An unattended bag found in the company’s offices contained Alfozan’s wallet and identification, as well as a second recording device, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in San Francisco.Alfozan has worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors said. He has been a legal permanent resident of the U.S. since Sept. 2020, court documents said.OpenAI personnel found the device Sept. 30. It was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room and had been concealed in toilet paper, the complaint says. The company determined it was installed around Sept. 28, and its contents were encrypted.Surveillance footage shows Alfozan near the room on multiple dates before the discovery, though he was not authorized to enter the room or attend meetings there, prosecutors said. Meetings in the room frequently involved confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and government engagements, according to the complaint.Prosecutors say this image shows Alfozan looking behind a television in an OpenAI conference room.​ | Source: Courtesy U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of CaliforniaBefore the device was installed, Alfozan used a productivity tool to ask about OpenAI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, room capacities, and calendars, as well as the locations of leadership and outside partner meetings, the complaint alleges.A chatbot account tied to Alfozan’s spouse, which shared identifiers with his own account, submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 about building, installing, obscuring, and remotely accessing a recording device, prosecutors said. Queries included how to “build a continuous audio recorder” and “encrypt the SD card,” prosecutors claimed. On Sept. 27 and 28, the account asked about the specific device that was later found, including its unique MAC address.“For us it is a matter of national security,” U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian said in a statement.On Oct. 5, the complaint says, Alfozan entered the conference room and appeared to look behind the television. That same day, he allegedly left a bag unattended in a printer. Security personnel who opened it found his wallet and ID, along with a second recording device similar to the first. He later reported that he’d misplaced the bag to company officials.OpenAI examined the device in the bag, which had a recording microcontroller and had been customized to obfuscate stored data, “such as potentially intercepted audio communications,” according to an FBI affidavit.When Alfozan retrieved the bag on Oct. 6, it no longer contained the device. He reported that his credit card, approximately $500, two AirPods, headphones, sunglasses and a power bank were stolen, but made no mention of the recording device, the affidavit said.The recording device with encrypted contents. | Source: Courtesy U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of CaliforniaFBI Director Kash Patel said protecting U.S. AI innovation is among the bureau’s highest counterintelligence priorities. Scott Schelble, special agent in charge of the FBI’s San Francisco field office, said the agency is committed to protecting sensitive research and proprietary technology.If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release. The case is being prosecuted by the National Security, Cyber & Special Prosecutions Section of the U.S. attorney’s office for the Northern District of California.OpenAI said on X (opens in new tab) that after discovering the device, employees used the company’s AI models to determine what it was and where it came from, and referred the matter to the FBI. The company thanked the agents and prosecutors who “moved quickly to make an arrest.”According to OpenAI, its technical surveillance countermeasures team found the device during a sweep of a conference room. OpenAI described the device as sophisticated and designed to evade detection, saying it had advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data in a way meant to avoid monitoring. The company said investigators used its models to analyze forensic images of the device’s storage and assess changes in the underlying data.Court documents filed by prosecutors identified the recording device as Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage. Amazon sells it for $23.99.The company said it has evidence that Alfozan intended to place other recording devices in sensitive spaces to secretly record meetings.According to OpenAI, Alfozan was a member of the product team. The company said it coordinated the timing of his firing with the FBI to avoid disrupting the investigation, and he was terminated Friday, the day he was arrested. Between Sept. 30 and that date, OpenAI said, it gradually restricted his access to systems and spaces, then suspended his physical and network access, placed him on leave, and secured his company-issued equipment.A YouTube video last month touted him as the only Saudi employee at OpenAI.“Honestly, this one year felt like five years anywhere else,” he said in response to a question about his experience.“The idea of AI is that it handles things one might not want to do, so they can focus on tasks or hobbies they enjoy more or work they take pleasure in and let it do the tedious tasks,” Alfozan said later in the video. A LinkedIn profile that matches Alfozan’s name lists his OpenAI role as engineering lead on the company’s AI agents platform.The resume said he has been a venture partner with Riyadh-based RAED Ventures since 2025. The company did not respond to The Standard’s inquiries.Before joining OpenAI,  he was a founding engineer at Nash, an AI infrastructure company for logistics, from 2022 to August 2025, according to the LinkedIn profile. From 2017 to 2022, he was a senior systems engineer at Meta. His earlier experience, according to the profile, includes a stint as a systems engineer at Reach Labs, a wireless power startup in Y Combinator’s summer 2015 batch, and internships at Microsoft, SAP in Berlin and Akamai Technologies.He has a master’s degree in data science from UC Berkeley, the LinkedIn profile says.A man in the passenger seat of a car at Alfozan’s Millbrae home said that the family did not want to speak to reporters.OpenAI said it has no indication that Alfozan improperly accessed or took model weights, source code, or customer data and has not seen activity that compromised the safety of its products or customers’ information. The company said it will continue to support the FBI’s investigation.OpenAI said it treats protecting its technology, data and people “as a matter of national importance” and called the case an example of how AI can counter sophisticated security threats.A detention hearing before U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse is set for Oct. 19.

articles.sourceTitle: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.text:
This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai, install DDoS code and other payloads? Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target. Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it.
“Such an ‘AI worm’ could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware,” Anthropic said. “Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.”
Anthropic called these autonomous worms small weight-based replicators. The models ran agents that had access to common exploitation tools, like reverse shells. The flow of the attacks was (1) finding targets, (2) gaining code execution, (3) establishing inference, and (4) propagating to new hosts. A key benefit over traditional worms is what Anthropic said is the agents’ ability to learn on the job. Each time an AI replicator fails to compromise a specific platform device, it can leave a list of prompts, code, and notes to future replicators so they don’t waste time reusing the same ineffective steps.

Credit:
Anthropic

Credit:

Anthropic

Anthropic said the dynamic inference setup is the least studied and likely most challenging stage in the replication cycle. It requires a long sequence of decisions based on the specific hardware and software of each target and involves selecting compatible inference software, installing dependencies, and debugging platform-specific bugs.
“These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from,” Anthropic said.

The experiment shows that small models are becoming increasingly capable at solving those problems autonomously. At the moment, however, none of the light-weight models tested are able to mount end-to-end replication, meaning discovering new devices, using an exploit to gain access to them, infecting them with a payload, configuring an inference server, and repeating the process. The process is also painfully slow; Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over the 15 Android TV boxes, performed at just 0.39 tokens per second. That translates to a full-inference setup time of 71 to 150 hours for an unoptimized Gemma4-26B-A4B and 29 to 51 hours for Qwen3.5-9B. (The researchers said that the large model GLM-5.2 appears to be able to do so reliably.)

articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic \ Anthropic
articles.text: At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026.In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.Growing our monorepoBefore we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.The typical setup for scaling git checkouts.Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?Principles for agent-scale source controlWith agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling, so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.How Scion worksIt’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.Data structuresIn Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent,1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.The shape of a changeset in Scion.This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.Scaling ScionA small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want.In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the sa

articles.sourceTitle: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary
articles.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. – Popcar's Blog
articles.text:
AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.

14 Oct, 2026

IntroductionI'm going to preface this post by saying I generally don't like AI. What an original take, I know. I hate that the internet is full of slop and bots, I hate that it's used as justification to fire hundreds of thousands of workers, I hate that the AI industry is making hardware inaccessible for consumers, I hate that it's being shoved into everything, and so forth. I like to do everything by my hand and take pride in my work.
That said, every now and then there's AI news that becomes impossible to ignore or act like it doesn't matter. This is especially one of those times. AI is now able to very quickly decompile video games and software, allowing them to easily get modified and enhanced and recompiled to all sorts of different systems.
And honestly? I have to admit - it's very cool. So many old, abandoned games are getting native ports to other platforms, enhanced with high FPS and running at dynamic native resolutions, with modding support. These type of enhancements usually aren't possible through an emulator.
Game Decompilations???Decompiling games and software is the process of reverse-engineering it from a compiled version back to source code. Once decompiled, you can practically do anything you want to that code then recompile it back to an executable that runs on your computer. Or mobile phone. Or smart fridge, really.
Decompiling old games isn't a new trend. The process of picking apart an old game and re-writing the code was doable by hand, but it was so complicated and time-consuming that it took years to decompile a game. The only ones that ever make it to the finish lines are through massive community efforts. Notable decompilations tirelessly made by hand are OpenGOAL (Jak and Daxter games) and Ship of Harkinian (Zelda Ocarina of Time/Majora's Mask). These developers are legends.
Thanks to the games being decompiled, modding all these games is now possible, and there are some really fun ones. Here's Jak and Daxter but you play as Gordon from Half Life. The mod can be found here, and it was not made with AI.

Newer AI models and workflows are now able to decompile games in a matter of days, or maybe less. The code isn't nearly as clean as doing it by hand, but it works. Some ports are a mess made by people who have no idea what they're doing, but most ports are undeniably impressive and stable.
Some ExamplesA great example of this being used for good is IsaacRecomp, which ports The Binding of Isaac in C++! No, not the remake. This is for the original Flash version made in 2011. Flash Isaac ran at a locked 30FPS and a low, blurry resolution. It was also a bit unstable because you're trying to run Adobe Flash in 2026. But now... Look at this.

The game now runs at a native 1440p, smoothly interpolated to 165FPS! If you've ever played Flash Isaac, you can immediately tell how beautiful that looks compared to the original. And it was all made automatically. In a few days. By an AI. That's insane.
There are hundreds of these projects now, with more coming every day. From a game preservation standpoint, it's incredible how we can take old janky experiences and get them to play on modern systems while also modernizing them. You can absolutely have your opinions regarding AI, but you have to admit this is cool.
Another one I like is Colin McRae Rally 2.0, a very old game that also barely ran on modern systems. Or Final Fantasy Tactics Advance, now running at any aspect ratio with dynamic zooming in and out. There's a Metroid Prime port. There's Ratchet and Clank which should be finished soon. There are too many more to mention and I'm struggling to keep track of them all.
The Scary PartMost people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entiry tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software.
Decompiling software is completely legal, and even if it won't be - it doesn't matter. You can't prove it's stolen code. I can make 1:1 copies of other things and say it's totally original, then publish it online. Someone made a fantastic joke website about how you can copy code with AI and claim it's made in a clean room, so technically you're not under any licensing agreements.
That's scary. The implications of this haven't been fully realized by people yet, but it's only a matter of time before alarms start ringing. I expect that in the next few months, we'll see some major application get decompiled and shared that will cause a serious response from companies.
Maybe open source licenses are completely unenforceable now. Maybe critical software and hardware can be easily hacked into now, and we haven't realized just how bad it is yet. Maybe everything will have more invasive DRM on it soon. Who knows. We're about to find out in the next few months.
But Isn't This Also Awesome?This is still a big win for consumers, though. Old abandoned games and software can be ported and polished for modern systems! I can't help but be giddy when seeing something like Skate 3 and Black Ops Zombies running on your browser. We live in weird times.

I wasn't kidding, here's Black Ops 1 Zombies running on my browser (at a bad framerate, but still)

This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. Shouldn't that be celebrated more?
There's a project in development called AnyPS5 which will allow you to automatically port any PS5 game to your PC, making them fully playable. This isn't hypothetical vaporware, some PS5 games have already been ported to PC such as Animal Well! This also isn't an emulator, it's more of a compatibility layer similar to Proton (which allows you to play Windows games on Linux).
With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks.
I expect modding become way easier too since AI can find ways to hook into a game's code. You might've already seen some sloppy mods that combine two games together. Those are dumb, but they make a point that AI could potentially create modding frameworks for previously unmoddable games. That's neat.
I know. AI still sucks, it's still causing a lot of issues in the world, and it's still accelerating us to a future that is too uncertain. But this is one of the positives of having such a technology, and I hope instead of random internet users attacking those using AI for decompilation and blindly hating these projects, we can just accept the win and play that old game you like at 4K 240FPS.

articles.title: Gemini — Google DeepMind
articles.text:
Slide 1 of 4Solving frontier problems with expertsResearchers, engineers, and security specialists are pairing with Argon to push the boundaries of science, math, robotics and cyber defense.Unlocking new scientific breakthroughsArgon is helping researchers at Google and the scientific community accelerate their path to discovery and real-world impact.Accelerating roboticsArgon autonomously turns raw video to a physics-accurate simulation, estimating depth and physical boundaries, and writing the exact simulation code required to replicate those real-world environments.Scaling cybersecurity defense responsiblyArgon ties for #1 on CWE-Bench (68%) for vulnerability remediation, is our most resilient model against indirect prompt injections, and is expanding to hundreds of additional Fairwind Program partners today.Untangling browser feature code in ChromeQuantum chemistry open-source package optimizationOptimizing a production Python codebase in hoursMaking our open Gemma models nearly three times as fast  At Isomorphic Labs, the team is using Argon as a partner to accelerate their drug discovery and design research workflows. Argon is able to quickly synthesize complex PDFs and patents to extract pertinent information, reducing a process that typically takes weeks into hours.Ambience HealthcareAmplitudeAxiom BioBoxCartwheelDeloitteKeplerLexisNexisMinutalAQuadrillionQuoraRoboflow “On over 200 complex synthetic longitudinal charts, Gemini 4 achieved the highest recall and ICD-10 code specificity among the models we evaluated, producing concise problem lists without external lookups. That combination of medical knowledge and long-context understanding shows promise for clinician-reviewed chart workflows. We're now validating it on real patient records and excited to try it out more broadly.”   “Argon is doing a great job at understanding what people actually mean. Customers collect endless signals that they don't know what to do with. Argon consistently scored amongst the top in our evals for building charts that help visualize the solutions for customers. It's also meaningfully persistent about finding those kinds of needle in a haystack answers that are valuable to customers.”Curtis LiuCTO, Amplitude   “Gemini 4 represents a step change in what AI can accomplish in real-world science. We've seen it reason through complex experimental data, from cellular imaging to mass spectrometry, and make subtle findings that traditionally require expert scientists to identify. On our Scientific Agent Benchmark, Gemini 4 was at the frontier across most tasks, including our hardest: ranking the clinical risk between two drugs.”Alex CabreraFounding Engineer, Axiom Bio   “Gemini 4 Argon is at the frontier of enterprise knowledge work, achieving a 14% improvement in accuracy compared to Gemini 3.1 Pro. In Box’s evaluation, Argon connected evidence across the full set of documents, including details embedded in figures, and carried multi-step analyses through to complete answers. This is especially valuable in data analysis and in technical fields like healthcare and life sciences, where teams need to find and interpret information across many kinds of source material.”Yashodha BhavnaniVP of AI Products at Box   “By integrating Gemini 4 into our 3D spatial reconstruction engine, we turn everyday video into articulated, physics-ready 3D scenes in seconds instead of hours. Across our benchmarks, Gemini outperformed every model we tested — cutting runtime nearly 100× and token usage by 90%, unlocking physics ready and watertight 3D asset creation for our customers.”Andrew CarrCo-founder and Chief Scientist, Cartwheel   “Early impressions from Gemini 4 are very strong: for long-running tasks across these workflows, it completed successfully 100% of the time in our evals, maintaining context and running through multiple tools across impressive spans. Its depth of reasoning delivers significantly higher, clearer output. Performing in-depth reasoning for domain-specific tasks without detailed prior logic or instructions is something we’ve never seen with any model in its class before.”Gopal SrinivasanGlobal AI and Data Lead, Deloitte   “On our core financial analysis benchmarks, which span building multi-year financial statements straight from SEC filings to valuing companies with complex capital structures and announced acquisitions, Gemini 4 matched our analyst-built reference models on more than 99% of figures. Performance on our most complex workflows was at the frontier in a majority of tasks. We're excited to keep building with Gemini 4 at Kepler.”Glenn LeBlancSoftware Engineer, Kepler   “To help legal professionals achieve more with Lexis+ with Protégé, we continuously evaluate AI models as part of the multi-model approach behind the LexisNexis Legal Intelligence Engine. In preliminary evaluations, Gemini 4 Argon demonstrated strong performance across legal knowledge, drafting, and analysis tasks, including identifying relevant citations and improving contract reviews, complaint analyses, and research memos.”Min ChenChief AI Officer, LexisNexis Legal & Professional   “In early testing, Gemini 4 Argon stood out by connecting dates, documents, and financial calculations with legal precedents to develop highly substantive arguments. In one evaluation, it actually surpassed our human expert's answer key by surfacing a legally relevant detail we had missed. This demonstrates AI’s potential to help professionals uncover crucial details and bring a more complete understanding to complex cases.”Caio PeronaCEO, MinutalA   “In Qualia, our autonomous AI researcher, Gemini 4 Argon has been a standout in our evaluations for both capability and efficiency. On our internal benchmarks of complex, multi-step research tasks, it performs at the frontier while completing our evals 1.5x faster than peer models at a quarter of the cost per task. It excelled at coming up with novel ideas and identifying non-obvious insights about the problem, helping it maintain a clear research vision over long horizons, something today's models struggle with.”Trenton ChangChief Scientist, Quadrillion   “Gemini 4 impressed us with the quality of its responses in our early evaluations. On Poe, people are increasingly using AI to build things, and Gemini 4 gives creators a powerful foundation for turning an idea into a tool they can refine and share.”Gareth JonesHead of Product, Quora   “Argon ranked first in our object detection evaluations and led our new text benchmark, which uses real-world images from manufacturing, logistics, and aerial imagery. We’ve fully integrated Argon into Roboflow so developers and enterprises can leverage its high precision detection and text extraction to inspect products, track inventory, and guide machines.”Brad DwyerCo-founder and CTO of Roboflow    To demonstrate these capabilities in action, we tested Argon’s ability to learn an out of distribution physical skill simply by watching. In an internal test, Argon watched a raw video of a human playing cornhole, mapped the spatial coordinates of the environment, and calculated the required whole-body joint movements. It then autonomously built the simulation code. When transferred onto Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid, the robot quickly sank seven consecutive shots in a real-world trial.  Wiz is already using Argon for its “Scan for Good” initiative, which protects critical public infrastructure for free. Having had early access to the model, Wiz used Argon to protect critical healthcare infrastructure. The model went beyond just spotting a vulnerability - it proactively safeguarded hundreds of thousands of patient records.
